### 2. Design Specs & Rules from `odd/tasks/p2-design.md`

* **Theme rules** (`p2-design.md:65-71`):
  * Dark "blueprint" (deep blue ground, light lines) + Light "paper" (warm, near-black ink, hairlines ≥ 3:1).
  * Default follows `prefers-color-scheme`. Real toggle button `<button id="theme" aria-pressed="...">` overrides via `localStorage`.
  * Tiny inline `<script>` in `<head>` applies `data-theme` before first paint (no flash).
  * Without JS: toggle is hidden, page follows OS scheme. Both themes pass WCAG AA (text ≥ 4.5:1, lines ≥ 3:1). Badge sits on dark surface in both.
* **Scroll rules** (`p2-design.md:73-80`):
  * Motion explains meaning, no scroll-jacking, no pinned sections taller than 1 viewport.
  * Progressive enhancement: script-driven `requestAnimationFrame` updating CSS custom properties (`--p`, `--prog`), with graceful fallback.
  * `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: all scroll animations disabled, final finished state rendered. Only animate `transform`, `opacity`, `stroke-dashoffset`.
* **Interactive background rules** (`p2-design.md:46-55`):
  * Faint drafting grid (`.bgfx`). On pointer hover, brightens in a soft radial circle (~220 px) with drafting crosshair (`.chx`, `.chy`) and monospace coordinate readout (`.xy`).
  * `pointer-events: none`, `z-index: 0` behind content. Only for `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`.
  * Single passive `pointermove` setting `--mx`, `--my` in `requestAnimationFrame`. Crosshair hides on interactive elements (`a, button, input...`), when pointer leaves, or on keydown.
* **Real links & shared content** (`p2-design.md:82-120`):
  * Verbatim texts, draft flags on Hero line & About paragraphs.

# P2 — design directions

Phase P2 of `BRIEF.md` §8. Ends at a gate: Teo picks one direction. Each
direction is one self-contained HTML artboard under `design/portfolio-directions/`.

## Specs

- S1: "Before building UI, propose **2–3 distinct directions** (static HTML artboards or screenshots) and stop for Teo to choose. Restraint: one typeface pairing, a small palette, motion only where it explains something."
- S2: "Theme: **personal story**. Thread: from a kid at a computer to an engineer who builds agents and robots. Let the aesthetic come from his real work (engineering drawings, kinematic diagrams, annotated notes), not from generic dev clichés."
- S3: "positioned on two legs: **software with AI / agents** and **hardware** (robotics, embedded). The site must make both visible from the hero onward, not hide hardware as a footnote."
- S4: "It must pass the recruiter "10-second test": who he is, what he builds, proof it is real, how to reach him. Original and pleasant, but never flashy or "vende humo": substance first, motion second."
- S5: "Saturated, avoid as the main idea: terminal/ASCII-everything aesthetics and "chat with my resume" bots."
- S6: "Targets: Lighthouse ≥ 95 in all categories on mobile, works without JS for all core content, `prefers-reduced-motion` respected, keyboard accessible, WCAG AA."
- S7: "**One** personal photo: childhood at the computer, as the origin anchor of the timeline. The other milestones (...) are text-only; do not use stock images or placeholders for them." Photo treatment (media/photos/photos.yaml): "Authentic, no generative AI enhancement or upscaling. Show it small (roughly 280-360 px wide on desktop), optionally cropped toward the child and keyboard. Allowed: ... a print-like frame or a subtle palette-matched treatment chosen in P2. Avoid feathered/blurred edges."
- S8: "Show the official **"Built with Gentle-AI" badge** ... in the footer, linking to the gentle-ai repo: ... keep its aspect ratio, size it to fit the footer (it may be smaller than 220 px), and check it reads well on the chosen palette. AI Hero has no badge: credit it as a text link next to it."
- S9: "Contact one click away on every page." Links: GitHub, LinkedIn, email (lightly obfuscated), DEV, CV PDF.

- S10 (L4): "I like the "Drafting sheet" style, but it gives the arm too much importance for my taste and the size of the project. Let's consider a similar approach but more general."
- S11 (L4): "Lab notebook is too simple, so is "Two legs" is as well. Propose more and different options."
- S12 (L4): "I would like it to have some kind of interaction with the scroll if it's appropriate"

- S13 (L6): "they all feel too bright and washed out"; themes per L7: "Follow system + toggle".
- S14 (L7): combine 04 Drawing set + 05 Exploded view.

- S15 (L8): "Keep only the 'Cover and sheets' and 'Exploded index' versions, but polish them a bit"
- S16 (L8): "fix the scroll effect, as it currently isn't showing up in either of them"
- S17 (L8): "I'd like an interactive background effect where it reacts when the mouse hovers over it"

## Interactive background rules (S17)

- Same effect in both artboards: the page background is a faint drafting grid; under the mouse pointer the grid lines near the cursor brighten in a soft circle (radial mask, about 220 px), and a thin drafting crosshair with a small X/Y coordinate readout in monospace follows the pointer. It is the drawing language reacting to the reader, not decoration for its own sake.
- Behind all content (`pointer-events: none`, `z-index` below content); never lowers text contrast; never moves layout.
- Only for `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`. Touch devices, `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and no-JS get the static faint grid only. The crosshair hides when the pointer leaves the window or is over a link/button, and while the user types.
- Implementation: one `pointermove` listener (passive) that writes `--mx`/`--my` CSS custom properties in a `requestAnimationFrame`; the glow is a `mask-image: radial-gradient(...)` on a grid layer. No canvas, no per-frame layout reads.
- Works in both themes (grid colour from the theme tokens).

## Scroll fix rules (S16)

- Teo's machine: Windows animations are ON (`ClientAreaAnimation=True`) and the default browser is Chrome, so reduced motion and missing support are NOT the cause; the effects are broken.
- Diagnose by actually scrolling: launch the installed Chrome headless with remote debugging from a script in the OS temp dir (Node 22 has a global `WebSocket` for CDP), scroll to several positions (`window.scrollTo`), and read computed values (`getComputedStyle(el).transform`, `strokeDashoffset`, the title block text, `aria-current`) plus screenshots at each position. **1. "How I work with AI" → "My usual workflow"**

I wouldn't make this change. The new title drops "AI", and that word is what sets the section apart. It's also what a recruiter scanning the page is looking for. "Usual" makes it sound vague and casual. The section is about the setup you built around the agent, not your routine in general.

If you want something shorter or less formal, these keep the meaning:
- **"How I build with AI"** (my pick: it's active and fits "builds agents and robots")

The title appears in five places: the main nav, the parts list, the rail label, the home section heading and the page's own heading. It's a quick change whichever you pick.

**2. "CV" → "Resume"**

It depends on who you want to reach:
- **US and Canada:** "Resume" is the usual word. There, "CV" often means a long academic document.
- **UK, Europe and Latin America:** "CV" is normal.

You're aiming at remote roles. If most of those are US companies, use **"Resume"**. If the target is broader, keep "CV": it's shorter and everyone understands it. Whichever you choose, I'd use it everywhere: nav, page title, the "CV (PDF)" link, and the URL (`/resume/`, with `/cv/` redirecting to it). Which market are you mainly targeting?

## Problem

A developer who works with Claude Code all day sometimes wants to be examined out loud on a project they built, or to drive a coding session by voice. Socra is a local, private voice layer for that: the model speaks, you answer out loud, and the page shows only code, permission prompts or the reply.

## Constraints

- Private: the server binds to 127.0.0.1 only, and nothing leaves the machine except what Claude Code itself sends.
- Windows first. Python 3.12+, Node 22+, a microphone and Edge or Chrome. An NVIDIA GPU is optional; CPU works.
- A transcription budget of 3.0 s or less.
- The Piper voice model is about 79 MB.

## Problema

Quien trabaja con Claude Code todo el día a veces quiere que lo examinen en voz alta sobre un proyecto que construyó, o dirigir una sesión de programación por voz. Socra es una capa de voz local y privada para eso: el modelo habla, tú respondes en voz alta, y la página muestra solo código, solicitudes de permiso o la respuesta.

## Restricciones

- Privado: el servidor escucha solo en 127.0.0.1, y nada sale de la máquina salvo lo que envía el propio Claude Code.
- Primero Windows. Python 3.12+, Node 22+, un micrófono y Edge o Chrome. Una GPU NVIDIA es opcional; funciona con CPU.

## 2. Research Summary (~1.5k Tokens)

### 2.1 Project Overview & Purpose
Pricor is an open-source, local-first system designed to solve a ubiquitous and error-prone operational problem faced by small Argentine retail businesses (hardware stores, stationeries, kiosks, distributors): weekly supplier price lists arrive in heterogeneous Excel and CSV formats with erratic structures, unstandardized column headers, and missing or ambiguous business metadata.

Standard Point of Sale (POS) and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems require rigid tabular schemas. When store managers manually adjust spreadsheets or guess whether a price includes VAT, applies to a box of 100, or carries a chained distributor rebate (`10+5`), errors silently enter the catalog, corrupting profit margins. Pricor acts as a **local filter in front of the merchant's existing software**, standardizing diverse lists into a clean, normalized schema (`supplier_code, description, unit_cost_net, currency, vat_rate, units_per_pack, barcode, suggested_retail_price, source_row`) with row-by-row auditability.

### 2.2 Core Architectural Philosophy: Interpretation vs. Execution
Pricor's design is captured by its guiding motto:
> *"The models fill the form, the engine does the math, you sign."*

The architecture strictly segregates fuzzy natural-language interpretation from deterministic mathematical execution:
1. **Models never touch numbers and never execute code:** Large language models and fine-tuned tabular classifiers are untrusted context interpreters. They are constrained to proposing column roles from a closed set of 10 labels, suggesting answers to deterministic questions, or proposing schema field mappings.
2. **Deterministic execution via a closed operations catalog:** Calculations run strictly through an immutable Python `Decimal` engine with 50 digits of working precision (`ROUND_HALF_UP` rounding occurs exactly once at the end). The calculation follows a strict pipeline:
   $$\text{parse\_number} \rightarrow \text{apply\_discounts} \rightarrow \text{strip\_vat} \rightarrow \text{per\_unit} \rightarrow \text{convert\_currency} \rightarrow \text{final rounding}$$
3. **Auditability and adding-machine tape UI:** Every row processed generates an immutable `TraceStep` trail showing the raw input cell, each intermediate transformation, and the final net unit cost. In the web UI, this is presented as an adding-machine receipt tape (rendered in Azeret Mono), ensuring merchants can inspect the exact derivation of any cost.
4. **Local and private:** Designed for privacy and offline reliability. Nothing leaves the machine; all models run locally via Ollama and PyTorch. The only network call is an optional exchange rate lookup to DolarAPI, which can be completely replaced by manual entry.

### 2.3 The Three-Layer Classification Cascade
To map raw spreadsheet columns to semantic roles, Pricor implements a staged triage cascade calibrated on an independent validation set ($n=161$ columns) to enforce a target precision of $\ge 95\%$:
- **Profile (Deterministic):** Finds header rows, skips preambles/banners, infers number formats (decimal/thousands separators), and checks column data types without ML.
- **Layer 1 — Laya (Fine-tuned, Local):** A compact tabular column classifier fine-tuned on an RTX 4060 GPU (~6.2 GB VRAM peak, 290 s training) from the multilingual Laya base checkpoint. On CUDA, it infers in ~35 ms/column (~500 ms on CPU). If its confidence meets or exceeds $0.9959$, the role is settled automatically.
- **Layer 2 — Gemma 4 E4B (Local via Ollama):** For columns where Laya is unsure, Gemma classifies the remaining columns whole-sheet (~11.4 s/sheet on GPU). If Gemma's confidence is $\ge 0.9800$, it is settled automatically. Gemma also suggests answers to unstated list parameters.
- **Layer 3 — You (The Merchant):** Any column or parameter that fails the calibrated threshold escalates to the merchant with pre-filled recommendations. The merchant retains ultimate signing authority.

### 2.4 Verified Benchmark & Performance Metrics
Pricor avoids vanity metrics, publishing a rigorous benchmark on a held-out test set of 29 real columns from two unseen distributors (Dipel and DistriLap):
- **Standalone Accuracy:** Gemma achieved 86.2% (25/29), fine-tuned Laya achieved 75.9% (22/29), zero-shot Laya achieved 62.1% (18/29), and heuristic rules achieved 82.8% (24/29). *(Caveat: heuristic rules had seen Dipel headers during development, making the baseline optimistic).*
- **Cascade Behavior (Held-Out Set):** Under production thresholds, Laya auto-settles 10.3% (3 cols), Gemma settles 27.6% (8 cols), and 62.1% (18 cols) escalate to the user.
- **Automated Precision:** Of the 11 automatically settled columns, 10 were correct (**90.9% precision**). Of the 18 columns escalated to the user, the system's top recommendation was correct in 15 (83.3%), reducing user interaction to single-click confirmations.
- **Dormant Agreement Stage:** A stage designed to auto-settle when Laya and heuristics agree failed calibration (achieving only 88.0% precision on validation, below the 95% threshold). Pricor kept it dormant in the code rather than shipping an uncalibrated heuristic.
- **Zero Commercial Metrics:** The project explicitly documents that no paying customers, user interviews, or verified time-saving figures exist; claims of that nature are strictly prohibited.
